summary: The Green Orbit is an interactive agricultural decision-support platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It connects NASA Earth-observation data with local geographic and crop information to help farmers and planners make more informed, sustainable decisions. Users can search for a location, explore climate conditions such as temperature, rainfall, and solar radiation, view nearby agricultural infrastructure, and receive explainable crop and crop-rotation recommendations. The platform compares strategies based on water conservation, soil health, resilience, and yield outlook. By translating complex satellite and climate data into practical, location-specific insights, The Green Orbit helps address challenges such as changing rainfall patterns, rising temperatures, soil degradation, and limited access to agricultural information. It is important because it makes Earth intelligence more understandable and actionable while emphasizing that recommendations should complement—not replace—local farming expertise.
details:
## Project Details (THE GREEN ORBIT)>>>>

The Green Orbit is an interactive agricultural decision-support platform that transforms NASA Earth-observation data into practical, location-specific farming insights. Users can search for a city, country, region, or geographic coordinates, select locations through an interactive globe or map, and explore a complete agricultural profile.

The application retrieves climate signals from NASA POWER, including average temperature, rainfall, and solar radiation. These signals are analyzed alongside country crop data to identify suitable crops and calculate explainable climate-fit scores. The platform also provides crop-rotation recommendations based on user priorities such as water conservation and soil health. Users can compare strategies using indicators for water efficiency, soil improvement, resilience, and yield outlook.

An interactive Leaflet map displays the selected location and nearby agricultural, food, and circular-energy facilities sourced from OpenStreetMap. The project also integrates NASA imagery and Wikimedia Commons agricultural photographs to make the data more visual and understandable. Optional integrations support soil information through SoilHive, field identification through Varda, and crop-health analysis through EOSDA.

The project was developed as a web application using Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, React Leaflet, and REST APIs. It is designed to work in a standard desktop or mobile browser and does not require specialized hardware.

The project’s main benefit is that it makes complex climate and Earth-observation information accessible to farmers, planners, students, and communities. Instead of presenting raw satellite data, it connects environmental signals to practical questions such as what to plant, how to protect soil, and how to manage limited water resources.

The intended impact is to support more climate-resilient and sustainable agriculture, especially in regions affected by unpredictable rainfall, increasing temperatures, soil degradation, and limited access to agricultural expertise.

The project is creative because it combines a visual Earth interface, live climate data, crop intelligence, map-based infrastructure discovery, and an explainable rotation planner in one experience. The team considered data availability, regional differences, water demand, soil health, resilience, user accessibility, API limitations, and the need to clearly communicate that the recommendations are decision-support suggestions—not replacements for local farmers, agronomists, or extension experts.
